summary.text: Computing the initial terms gives \(a(5)=171\) and \(a(6)=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761\equiv57\pmod{108}\). Since \(2^{108}\equiv1\pmod{171}\) and \(2^{57}\equiv8\pmod{171}\), the next numerator is congruent to \(9\), not \(0\), modulo \(171\), so the required divisibility fails at \(n=7\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by showing that the recurrence first fails to produce an integer at the seventh term.

Let
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
As long as all preceding terms are integers, the next term is an integer exactly when
\[
a(n-2)\mid 2^{a(n-1)}+1.
\]
We calculate the first few terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=\frac{2^{a(2)}+1}{a(1)}=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,\\
a(4)&=\frac{2^{a(3)}+1}{a(2)}=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,\\
a(5)&=\frac{2^{a(4)}+1}{a(3)}=\frac{2^9+1}{3}=\frac{513}{3}=171.
\end{aligned}
\]
The sixth term is therefore
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
This is indeed an integer. To see this without evaluating the enormous power, note that powers of 2 modulo 9 have period 6, since \(2^6\equiv1\pmod 9\). As \(171\equiv3\pmod6\),
\[
2^{171}\equiv2^3=8\equiv-1\pmod9.
\]
Thus 9 divides \(2^{171}+1\). Denote this integer by
\[
N:=a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
Its decimal expansion is
\[
N=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761,
\]
but only a small congruence class of \(N\) will be needed.

We next prove
\[
N\equiv57\pmod{108}.
\]
Because \(9N=2^{171}+1\), it is enough to compute \(2^{171}+1\) modulo
\(9\cdot108=972\). Factor
\[
972=4\cdot243,
\]
where 4 and 243 are coprime.

Modulo 4, clearly
\[
2^{171}\equiv0\pmod4.
\]
We compute the residue modulo 243 by repeated squaring. First,
\[
2^9=512\equiv26\pmod{243}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{18}&\equiv26^2=676\equiv190\pmod{243},\\
2^{36}&\equiv190^2=36100\equiv136\pmod{243},\\
2^{72}&\equiv136^2=18496\equiv28\pmod{243}.
\end{aligned}
\]
(The reductions are \(676=2\cdot243+190\), \(36100=148\cdot243+136\), and \(18496=76\cdot243+28\).) Hence
\[
2^{81}=2^{72}2^9\equiv28\cdot26=728\equiv-1\pmod{243},
\]
since \(728=3\cdot243-1\). Now \(171=2\cdot81+9\), so
\[
2^{171}=(2^{81})^2 2^9\equiv(-1)^2\cdot26=26\pmod{243}.
\]
The four residues modulo 972 that are congruent to 26 modulo 243 are
\[
26,\ 269,\ 512,\ 755.
\]
Of these, only 512 is divisible by 4. Since \(2^{171}\) is divisible by 4, the two congruences just obtained imply
\[
2^{171}\equiv512\pmod{972}.
\]
It follows that
\[
9N=2^{171}+1\equiv513=9\cdot57\pmod{972}.
\]
Thus \(972=9\cdot108\) divides \(9(N-57)\). Cancelling the nonzero integer factor 9 gives
\[
108\mid N-57,
\]
and therefore
\[
N\equiv57\pmod{108}.
\]
In particular, for some nonnegative integer \(q\),
\[
N=108q+57.
\]

We now determine \(2^N\) modulo the denominator \(a(5)=171\). Factor
\[
171=9\cdot19,
\]
with 9 and 19 coprime. First we show that
\[
2^{108}\equiv1\pmod{171}.
\]
Modulo 9, \(2^6\equiv1\), and 6 divides 108, so \(2^{108}\equiv1\pmod9\). Modulo 19, Fermat's theorem gives \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}\), and 18 divides 108, so \(2^{108}\equiv1\pmod{19}\). Since 9 and 19 are coprime, an integer congruent to 1 modulo both is congruent to 1 modulo their product. Hence
\[
2^{108}\equiv1\pmod{171}.
\]

Similarly,
\[
2^{57}\equiv8\pmod{171}.
\]
Indeed, \(57=9\cdot6+3\), so modulo 9,
\[
2^{57}\equiv2^3=8\pmod9.
\]
Also \(57=3\cdot18+3\), so Fermat's theorem modulo 19 gives
\[
2^{57}\equiv2^3=8\pmod{19}.
\]
Again using the coprimality of 9 and 19, these two congruences combine to give \(2^{57}\equiv8\pmod{171}\).

Since \(N=108q+57\), we conclude that
\[
2^N=2^{108q+57}=(2^{108})^q2^{57}\equiv1^q\cdot8=8\pmod{171}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2^{a(6)}+1=2^N+1\equiv8+1=9\pmod{171}.
\]
The residue is 9 rather than 0. Consequently,
\[
171\nmid 2^{a(6)}+1.
\]
But \(a(5)=171\), so at the seventh recurrence step the required divisibility is precisely
\[
a(5)\mid2^{a(6)}+1,
\]
and this divisibility fails. Equivalently,
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{a(5)}
     =\frac{2^N+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer. Thus not every term generated by the recurrence is an integer, disproving the conjecture.
